glossary.title: What is ReinvestOne?
glossary.llm_summary: Kevin of the channel Meet Kevin promotes 'Reinvest One', a single-price subscription bundle that includes the Alpha Report (daily short, medium and long-term outlook covering technical and fundamental views), trade alerts, portfolio transparency alerts, private live streams, and nine courses on topics such as stock investing, real estate, YouTube passive income and AI. He says the company has 58,000 members since 2018 and 11,000 repeat buyers. Lifetime access is offered only if bought before 2027, after which sales move to recurring subscriptions. A new 'stocks terminal' launches in December 2026, pitched as an aggregator of balance sheet, pricing power, momentum and valuation data, with a Bloomberg comparison at about $2,500 a month. A homes terminal and AI blueprints follow in 2027. He cites compute and data-licence costs of tens of thousands to over $100,000 a month, but gives no market data, macro views or asset-price forecasts.

glossary.llm_summary: Felix Nicholas Pin, a self-described economist and former investment banker, says the SEC granted Wall Street temporary exemptive relief from the locate rule for short sales made outside regular trading hours. He says it was approved within one business day and runs to end-2027. He links this to US stock trading moving to roughly 23 hours a day, five days a week, from early December, which he argues will create sharp, thinly traded overnight moves. He cites several stocks rising over 1,000% in a minute pre-market this year but gives no source. On silver, he says spot is down about 65% from its high, the largest drop on record, while physical supply is tightening and paper prices fall. He points to the 200-day moving average, noting that deep discounts in 2014 and 2020 were followed by long-run rallies, and says rising selling volume can mark capitulation. He cites a VIX-style fear index at 28, having touched 35 intraday, and argues markets tend to bottom on bad news. He says the Nasdaq is now down on the year and that AI hardware is overcrowded. He expects 2027 leadership from AI-monetising platforms such as Meta, Google, Microsoft and Amazon, with caution on Oracle, supported by cash-flow and stability metrics from his app. He argues value stocks are neglected and calls PayPal's declining margins and low insider ownership a warning sign. Much of the video promotes a free Saturday seminar and a subscription app, and several headline claims come without primary data.

glossary.llm_summary: Host Kevin Praath (Meet Kevin) argues the stock market may be near a bottom and that recession signals are not yet flashing. His main gauge is Anthropic's post-IPO price action: shares listed around $83, rose to roughly $115, dipped to about $73, and have stayed above the -10% and -20% lines from the IPO price, closing near $84. He argues Anthropic carries less leverage (margin, options, leveraged ETFs) than Micron, SanDisk, Amazon, Meta or Microsoft, so it is a cleaner liquidity test. Macro data he cites: Q3 US GDP second read at 4.3% with personal consumption at 4.2%, continuing jobless claims well below the rest of the chart, stable-to-rising quit rates, and an Atlanta Fed Q4 GDP estimate of 2.9%. He says building permits fell 7.2% year-over-year, twice expectations, and that the 2-year Treasury yield rose after being down about six basis points intraday. On geopolitics, a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Ras Tanura facility, which he attributes to Houthis funded by Iran, lifted oil about 3.6% to roughly $94, and he describes US Navy escorts for Strait of Hormuz transits. He says tariffs on Asian and European partners are rising to two to three times prior levels and warns of a possible 50bp Fed move. On Nvidia, he reports a negative credit watch with a possible downgrade within 90 days from double-A, and Nvidia credit default swaps near 142 versus Meta near 118. Sponsor and course promotion is omitted.

glossary.title: The Coming 2027 Housing Market Disaster.
glossary.llm_summary: Kevin Paffrath, a US financial YouTuber and founder of the real-estate firm Reinvest, argues a US housing squeeze is building. He cites Redfin data showing the 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.21%, up from 6.23% a year earlier, and a nationwide median sale price of about $388,634, roughly $8,000 above the May 2022 peak and up 0.7% year over year. He cites a chart of pending home sales at record lows, with existing-home sales possibly the weakest since the mid-1990s. Single-family permits for October 2026 fell year over year in all four regions: West down 21.7%, Northeast down 19%, Midwest down 9.8%, South down 9.7%. He links this to data-centre construction rising about 90% in a year while home building fell 8.9%, says some data centres are outbidding builders for land in Northern Virginia, and cites Oxford Economics on builders exiting. He cites a Federal Reserve note arguing that productivity shocks, potentially from AI, lower Treasury yields and short rates over time. He also says UAE departure from OPEC and an oil surplus could push energy prices and rates down. He forecasts a squeeze for buyers around end-2028, since permits lead completions by about two years, and expects rates to be lower than in 2022 by 2032. On policy, he says Democratic-trifecta states issued about 2.6 permits per 1,000 people versus 4.2 for Republican-trifecta states, using 2025 Census-based data. He contrasts Hartford, up 28% from its 2022 peak, with Austin, down 28.8%, which issued about eight times Hartford's permits. Much of the transcript is promotional and auto-transcribed with errors, and several figures lack named primary sources.

Kevin Praat of the Meet Kevin channel argues the recent sell-off is deleveraging rather than the start of a recession, while conceding downside risk. He says Nvidia rose about 32% in one day (roughly $1 trillion of value) and then gave back about half of that gain, and that Nvidia fell about 8% in a later session. He cites a Barron's technical signal suggesting the Nasdaq 100 could retest its March lows in the 550-570 range and the S&P 500 could test 6,400-6,500, with about half of S&P 500 names still above their 50- and 200-day moving averages. He describes sentiment as extreme fear: a greed-and-fear index at 9, a put/call ratio of 0.94, and Wells Fargo data showing dealer gamma at the 6.7th percentile.

On trade, he says the administration announced higher tariffs: China possibly from 10% toward 20% or up to 40%, Vietnam to 35%, Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan to 25%, and EU rates expected to double. He notes only three of about 90 targeted trade deals were completed last year. He also reports new US licensing requirements for advanced chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil.

glossary.llm_summary:
Meet Kevin (published 25 Nov 2026) walks through a Wednesday tech selloff and the macro backdrop, with his own positioning. Equity data cited: the Nasdaq 100 down about 3% (at one point 3.6%) after bouncing near Friday's low; the Philadelphia semiconductor index down about 6.3%; Nvidia down about 7-8%, having given back roughly half of Monday's gain (he cites about a 32% one-day rise and roughly $1 trillion of value added); SpaceX down about 7.8% to around $115, near its IPO price; Micron reported more than 50% below its peak. Anthropic, recently IPO'd, is down about 1% and holding a 20% drawdown line on his chart, which he attributes to leverage not yet having built up in the stock.

Rates: the 2-year yield is around 3.46%, down about 7.5bp, and the 10-year is down about 8bp. He argues the 2-year sitting roughly 100bp above the 3.5% levels seen during the 2024 carry-trade and late-2025 labour scares signals no recession pricing, and that the Fed is still expected to hike, with a December hike referenced. He cites ADP private payrolls above 20K and ISM and S&P PMIs still showing hiring. He says Wells Fargo data puts dealer gamma positioning at the 6.7th percentile, which amplifies moves. Sentiment gauges cited: a fear index of 9 and a put/call ratio near 0.94. He cites Kalshi pricing implying very little chance of an unchanged Fed path this year.

Trade policy: he describes a 'Liberation Day 2.0' tariff push. China would go from 10% to 20%, possibly 40%; the EU to 20%; Vietnam to 35%; Cambodia, Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan to 25%. He says the 2025 '90 deals in 90 days' produced about three deals. He also cites a Brooklyn federal jury finding Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including trade-secret conspiracy and sanctions violations.

Iran and oil: tanker attacks continue, including an LNG carrier reportedly hit by a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. Oil has fallen about $25 from a four-week peak of $117 a barrel. He cites an agency projection of supply surplus of 1.7 mb/d in Q4 2026 and 3.8 mb/d in 2027, and says the UAE has left OPEC, which he treats as freeing output.

AI compute: a Semianalysis note reportedly says SpaceX cut Blackwell spot GPU rental from $15 to $10-12 per hour, and that Anthropic, said to be nearly a third of SpaceX's revenue, may not extend its compute contract beyond mid-2027. He reads this as the GPU scarcity premium fading, but says the note still expects SpaceX to keep expanding capacity. Dell's COO reportedly said there is no sign yet of enterprise NAND or DRAM price declines. BNP Paribas reportedly cut Micron to neutral with a target of $775, down from $1,700. He cites Oracle CDS at highs above their October peak, and CoreWeave 2030 bonds at about 74-76 cents, yielding near 18%.

Forecasts: a Barron's technical reading suggests the Nasdaq 100 could retest 550-570 and the S&P 500 6,400-6,500 within about 30 days, since over half of S&P 500 names remain above their 50- and 200-day averages. He cites a Fed note finding productivity shocks lower long-term yields, and expects 30-year mortgage rates near 1.8% in the 2030s. He says he is adding to stocks from a 3-5% allocation and buying real estate, at roughly $10 into property for each $1 in stocks. He has been bearish gold since its January peak, and says the gold selloff is a fire sale.

Several segments are paid sponsor reads (Investing Pro, Kalshi, a newsletter). He dismisses a WSJ report that US intelligence found no evidence China directed the Nvidia executive affair, calling it spin.

glossary.title: Pierre Lassonde: The Discovery of Three Lifetimes
glossary.llm_summary:
Podcast interview with Pierre Lassonde, co-founder of Franco-Nevada, former Newmont president and former World Gold Council chair. Most of the content is historical, but it includes several claims relevant to ASX-listed explorers and the royalty and gold markets.

Franco-Nevada origins: Lassonde says the company's first deal was a Gold Strike royalty bought for about US$2m, roughly the entire treasury, after a small classified ad in the Reno Gazette. After the discovery of around 50 Moz, the stock rose from about 65c to $16. He says geologist Brian Mikkelson told him it was 'the discovery of three lifetimes', which led the founders to keep building the company rather than sell.

Late 1990s: with gold at roughly US$250-300 and little mine development, Franco bought royalties and, through a tax-driven Nevada exploration programme, found the Ken Snyder deposit. That led to the Normandy stake and a bidding war with Anglo, and ultimately the Newmont merger in 2002. Lassonde says the royalty portfolio was neglected while he ran Newmont (roughly 2002-07), which left room for Wheaton and Royal Gold to emerge.

Gold ETF: he describes creating the GLD ETF over about 18 months at roughly US$12-15m in legal costs. He cites holdings above 3,000 tonnes and about 13% compounded annual growth over 22 years.

Royalty economics: he says royalties have more operating leverage than operators because they carry no costs. He argues that DCF undervalues mines because it ignores price and land optionality beyond about 15 years. He says Franco's reserves were depleted over a decade but replaced, moving from about 10 Moz reserve and 20 Moz resource to 15 Moz and 30 Moz.

Lassonde curve: built from a study of about 3,000 companies over a decade. The lowest-risk point is once financing is in place and a mine is being built. He says permitting has stretched from about 2 years to 5-7 years, which he calls the 'killing field'. He illustrates this with a US$10bn project that is worth nothing when discounted at 8% over 12 years. He notes that Canadian and US governments are moving to shorten approvals.

Current holdings he discusses: Southern Cross Gold's Sunday Creek project in Victoria, which he says has at least 4-5 Moz at roughly 8-10 g/t gold-equivalent with antimony, and which he thinks could produce about 200,000 oz a year. Atex, a copper-gold project he says has 1.5-2bn t of inventory, with 50-100 Mt at about 2% CuEq, two-thirds copper. Also Orla's Camino Rojo and Equinox. His stated lesson is that a few large winners pay for many losses, and that he holds about five positions at a time.

glossary.llm_summary: US equities are described as in a garden-variety pullback, with the S&P 500 near 6,700 and no recession or growth-scare signal yet. GPU rental prices are cited as rising: H100 rental rates are up 29% year on year and 47% over the first ten days of November, per Silicon Data. The speaker attributes this to demand from enterprise AI adoption and open-weight models running on older chips. A Goldman note is recalled as showing about 68% of token usage going to open-weight models while over 70% of spend goes to closed-weight models. Bernstein is cited with buy or outperform ratings and price targets on Apple, Western Digital, Seagate, Dell, SanDisk and Bloom Energy, arguing these stocks are overly punished. Wells Fargo is cited as saying capex fears are largely priced in, with a Fed hike into a recession scare as the main risk. Deutsche Bank is cited as saying volatility shocks typically take 6 to 8 weeks to bottom. RBC is cited as saying it is unclear the bottom is in and that new index highs may slip into 2027. Bloomberg is cited as saying recession evidence is absent and the selloff is multiple compression: the Nasdaq forward P/E is about 23.3x against a 24x average, with 2022's low at 20.4x. A chart is used to show stocks falling as expected Fed rate hikes rise, summarised as 'don't fight the Fed'. JP Morgan data is cited showing stocks higher 6 to 12 months after elections in every instance since 1950, and midterm years are described as weak with years three and four historically stronger. Much of the content is promotional (membership sales, Black Friday offers), and it includes a story about Nvidia's CEO returning after an ethics apology, which has limited market relevance here.
glossary.transcript_text: Well, folks, the market is crashing so badly, we're just now hearing that Jensen is in therapy nearly daily for an hour and a half because he's quote made some terrible mistakes. Who knows what it could be? But anyway, look at this. glossary.title: Trump is F**KING us Again.
glossary.llm_summary: Kevin, a YouTube analyst, says reports he attributes to the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg, with unconfirmed timing, point to new targeted Section 301 tariffs on China, the EU and about a dozen other economies, possibly announced soon after a month-long USTR investigation led by Greer. He frames this as 'Liberation Day 2.0', noting that Section 122 and 232 tariffs could be combined to rebuild country-specific rates. He states the trade-weighted US tariff rate was about 2.2% before Trump and is about 10% now, and traces Canada, China and EU rates from April 2025 to February 2026 after a Supreme Court loss. On data, he cites the Conference Board consumer confidence index at 103.3 for November, up from 91 in October and above a 92.4 expectation, with the labour-market differential up 12.4 points and business expectations at 83.6 from 74. He cites ADP private payrolls at 21,000 versus 23,000 the prior week, and argues the economy shows no sign of a layoff recession. On markets, he says the Nasdaq fell about 3% after a 7% gain the prior day, which Goldman Sachs calls a short squeeze, with no late-day buying. He expects the Fed to deliver a 25bp hike on 9 December, possibly ending its cycle. He reports Brent back under $90 as Omani exports offset Strait of Hormuz disruption, Houthi strikes injuring 11 in Saudi Arabia, and NBC reporting US officials debating strikes on Iranian leaders. He cites a Barron's view that the Nasdaq may not bottom until gold finishes correcting, and says 10-year yields and inflation expectations are easing. Several figures were spoken quickly and may be transcription-affected.

glossary.llm_summary:
Retail commentator Kevin (Meet Kevin, promoting his paid 'Reinvest' terminal) runs through the Monday 24 November 2026 session. The biggest in-scope item is trade policy. He cites WSJ and Bloomberg reporting that the US is preparing Section 301 tariffs on China, the EU and about 14 other economies, with announcements possibly within days. He says the reporting suggests tiered rates, with countries that have trade deals at 15% or lower and China possibly higher. He notes that Bloomberg had earlier reported a 7.5% rate on China, which would bring its total to 20%. He describes the current baseline as roughly 10% across the board, against a trade-weighted tariff of about 2.2% before 2025. He also says the Section 301 process requires a study and public comment, and that the public-comment deadline is not a binding waiting period. He argues this could take the market back toward 'Liberation Day' levels, and says the uncertainty is weighing on stocks.

On rates and macro, he reports that the Conference Board consumer confidence index rose to 103.3 in November from about 91 in October, with the expectations index at 83.6 against 74. He says the labour-market differential improved by 12.4 points and reads this as a sign against a layoff-led recession. ADP private payrolls came in at about 21,000 against 23,000 previously. He says the Fed is widely expected to hike 25 basis points at its 9 December meeting, with possibly one more move after that. He gives no source for that expectation.

He says Goldman Sachs described the previous day's Nasdaq surge of roughly 7% as a short squeeze, with little late-session buying. He cites a Barron's argument that gold may be signalling a Nasdaq bottom, with equities unlikely to bottom until gold finishes correcting. He says gold is under $3,600, Brent is back under $90 as Oman exports rise from outside the Strait of Hormuz, and Bitcoin is under $60k. He says Oman's growth is about 4.5% this year. He reports NBC News saying administration officials are debating targeting Iranian leaders, on top of existing naval and land blockades.

On equities, he is focused on Anthropic, which he says has broken through $77 on its second test after the IPO. He says his own floor is a 10 to 20% decline and that he has not bought the stock. He is positive on consumer discretionary names, citing Target, Eli Lilly and Apple, which he says rose on the day after he flagged them in an internal note. He also says Nvidia reversed about 7% after a roughly 31% surge the previous day. He reports Sandisk, post-split, and a Stripe tender offer valuing the company above $200bn. He reports Financial Times coverage of a possible Tesla–SpaceX merger, with a combined value of about $3.5tn and a push to finish by year-end. He cites prediction-market odds of about 43 to 64% for a deal by year-end.

Most of the rest is channel promotion, sponsor pitches and personal anecdotes, which I've left out. Figures are the speaker's own readings of news reports and charts, and several (the Fed hike expectation, the gold and oil levels, the Anthropic price levels) are not independently sourced in the transcript.

glossary.title: The Anthropic IPO Was Never About the Money
glossary.llm_summary: The speaker reviews Anthropic's S-1 filing after its IPO, which he describes as valuing the company above $1 trillion. He reports quarterly revenue more than 12 times the prior year's, running at about $81 billion annualised. The IPO plus a concurrent private sale raised about $85 billion, leaving roughly $213 billion in cash and investments. The main stated use is compute: about $900 billion of multi-year contracts running to 2045, with about $71 billion due in the next 12 months and about $450 billion before end-2030. Anthropic's direct borrowing is about $6 billion, all from Amazon and convertible into equity. A balance-sheet figure above $130 billion reflects marking that loan to the share price. The speaker says roughly $98 billion of chip financing sits in special purpose vehicles that buy Broadcom chips and lease them to Anthropic. Broadcom reportedly backstops two of these loans, with potential exposure of about $72 billion. He calls this circular financing, a term he attributes to the Federal Reserve's November stability report. He cites Anthropic's risk factors acknowledging dependence on partners' third-party credit. Its credit line reportedly rose from $2.5 billion to $15 billion, with collateral release tied to an investment-grade rating on its own unbacked debt. Net worth reportedly moved from negative $150 billion in September to positive $108 billion after the IPO. Broadcom's CEO said on September 2 that Anthropic's investment credit would change after the IPO. The speaker cites SpaceX, which reportedly received investment-grade ratings six days after its June listing, as a precedent. His thesis is that the IPO is the route to self-funded borrowing for the AI buildout. Relevance to the scope is indirect, through credit conditions, risk sentiment and AI-capex demand. The sponsor segment is excluded.

glossary.title: They're About to Reset Stocks, Gold and Silver
glossary.llm_summary: Felix Nicholas Pin, a self-described economist and founder of the Pin Institute, argues that the US government has become the implicit backstop of the AI sector after Nvidia reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as a board director. He says Nvidia gained $954 billion in market value in one day, about 31%, roughly double the prior record held by Microsoft at about $449 billion, and attributes the move to the board's own losses. He reads from a research note he attributes to a large Wall Street firm, calling it 'AI's first bailout.' He cites a Fed governor, Williams, saying 2027 will bring lower inflation, and argues rates could go sideways or fall next year, which would weaken the dollar and support gold. He shows a dollar chart and says the dollar is strengthening, a headwind for gold. He reports that CME raised gold margins from 5% to 6% and silver margins from 8% to 9.9%, forcing leveraged holders to sell. He says Turkey has already sold a lot of gold to support its lira. He expects short-term headwinds for gold and silver but says he is long both over the long term, and that nobody knows where prices go in the short term. He notes Huang testifies before the Senate Banking Committee on 3 December. The video also promotes a free PDF and a free Saturday Zoom seminar, and claims Goldman Sachs' 2027 gold report has gone to institutional clients. Most of the content is rhetorical. Several figures, including the Nvidia move, the Fed quote and the Turkey sales, are stated without sources in the transcript.

glossary.llm_summary:
The transcript is a live Q&A from the 'Meet Kevin' channel (published 2026-11-24, titled 'Beer w/ Kevin Q&A & Jensen Returns'), hosted by a US retail-investing personality who sells courses and a subscription. The opening segment is a repeated clip of meme-stock chanting and a quote about GameStop short interest and retail investors. The rest is the host's chat, and the macro-relevant material is limited and mostly unsourced.

Leverage: the host says the market is highly leveraged, citing FINRA margin debt at its highest level in September and second-highest in October. He argues leveraged ETFs, with fees up to 105 to 150 basis points, will eventually go to zero. He favours low-cost broad index funds and cites a Vanguard-style fund with Apple and Nvidia each around 13% and Google around 8%.

Nvidia and AI: he frames Jensen Huang's return as a key-person-risk story and says Nvidia is worth well over $300 eventually, with the AI bubble 'early stage'. He says a sale by Kathy Wood near the recent low reflected key-person concerns. He also argues that Nvidia and AMD chips are commodity-like and could end up in drones. He expects the AI buildout to continue, including enterprise demand such as Dell's.

Oil: he says WTI is under $80 and oil is back under $90 a barrel. He attributes this to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and a possible ongoing blockade around Iran, with other producers raising supply. He forecasts a potential oil supply glut in 2027 and says the market must adjust to that. He cites no data source.

Bitcoin: he says BTC is back under $60,000 and that CoinGlass data shows roughly $1 billion in liquidations over 24 hours. He treats the 82 level as lost and says a recovery is uncertain.

Copper: he says copper has become cheaper, which he reads as bearishness on the AI buildout, though he does not expect that buildout to slow.

Rates, labour and inflation: he says the 10-year yield (transcribed as '527', so likely 5.27%) guides mortgage rates and that he hopes it has peaked. He expects a future recession to be an unemployment recession but says current labour data does not show one, pointing to ADP weekly data (about 23.9K last week). He says PCE is derived from CPI and PPI and rarely moves markets.

Other: he says Nphase trades around $20 and, on his own calculation, shows roughly a 7% cash-flow yield. The rest covers real estate, car and aircraft purchases, and promotion for his course and a Black Friday offer. Specific prices and figures are his own and were not independently verified in the transcript.

glossary.title: What Trump JUST Said!
glossary.llm_summary:
Commentator Kevin Pra (Meet Kevin channel) reviews a claimed CNBC interview with Donald Trump about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. He says Trump said Huang was forced out by the board rather than resigning, that Trump phoned the board after Nvidia's stock fell about 50%, and that Trump was worried Huang could be hired by a rival such as China. Per the speaker, Nvidia lost about $2.8 trillion in market value, from roughly $5 trillion to $3 trillion, and Semafor reported Trump joined a board meeting, which the speaker says Trump did not deny. The same interview allegedly included Trump saying he is inclined to resume strikes on Iran after the new year if no deal is reached. The speaker describes a triple blockade on Iran (Strait of Hormuz, Caspian Sea, land borders) and says the strike threat was timed to distract from the Huang news. He calls this insider-trading-adjacent but labels it an allegation without evidence.

On macro data, he cites S&P Global November flash PMIs: output and order growth moderating, backlogs building, implied Q4 GDP growth around 3% annualised, employment still rising, and supplier delivery times lengthening most since August 2022. He cites US labour data showing the unemployment rate falling while participation rose, Black unemployment declining, and the 27-plus-week unemployed count flat since mid-2025. He attributes to Bloomberg the view that the usual recession evidence is missing. He also cites S&P Global Market Intelligence that AI infrastructure firms issued $212 billion of stock through October, and a Wall Street Journal piece saying the AI buildout is crowding out other sectors, including housing.

On rates, he says the Fed is likely to hike in December and then pause, and that 2% inflation is too low given geopolitics and AI capex. He attributes a similar 3% view to Bill Ackman (transcribed as 'Bill Aman') and cites Ackman's warning that financial conditions have tightened sharply, with SpaceX's secured debt priced near 8.25%. He warns that quarterly mark-to-market losses on securities holdings, such as Nvidia's and AMD's stakes, will hit reported EPS. He is bullish on AI and chips, bearish on consumer discretionary valuations, and bullish on real estate.

The transcript is heavily promotional: it repeatedly pitches the presenter's paid subscription products, a venture fund he says paid him to promote, and a sponsoring prediction market, and he reports his own trading gains. Those promotions carry no analytical weight here. The Iran, Huang and PMI claims are the parts relevant to the scope, and the Huang and Iran items rest on a secondhand account of an interview, not a primary source.

glossary.title: Jensen is OFFICIALLY BACK!!! Nvidia!!
glossary.llm_summary: Commentator Kevin Pratt, citing Nvidia's press release, reports that Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president and CEO with immediate effect, with Colette Kress continuing as CFO. He says Nvidia's stock fell about 14% the prior Friday on SEC investigation worries, and that Nvidia guided revenue of about $130 billion, plus or minus 3%. He cites a Fox Business report that President Trump publicly urged the board to rehire Huang. He also says Trump has backed away from renewed Iran strikes, and that the board formed a national security and export control committee and is searching for a chief compliance officer. He reports that the ARM CEO reportedly turned down a role at Nvidia. He argues the selloff is a buying opportunity for Nvidia and for the broader market, even after a reported 30% rebound. The content is largely promotional and speculative about motives, with few independent sources.

glossary.llm_summary: In a video dated 22 November 2026, Kevin Papra (Meet Kevin) reviews a sharp US equity sell-off. He cites the Nasdaq down 10.02% in the week, its worst since March 2020, and the S&P 500 down 8.6% to 6910 after seven straight losses. He says the chip index fell 17%, its worst week since September 2021, and Taiwan's market fell 17%. Nvidia fell 14% on Friday, which he puts at roughly half a trillion dollars of market value. The VIX rose 16.5 points in a week, the fifth-largest weekly jump on record. He reports several institutional views. JP Morgan says losses are driven by beta rather than alpha, and hedge-fund selling has not yet hit its capitulation trigger. Barclays expects about 50% of S&P 500 earnings in 2027-28 to come from chips and says a Fed reversal is needed. UBS says AI adoption is still early, with 8% of enterprises deploying AI agents at scale. Goldman Sachs says technicals have broken down, with 38 S&P 500 stocks up and 464 down on Friday, and that the market may be nearing a tactical low. The next catalyst is November CPI on 10 December. Bank of America is cited as seeing peak rates no earlier than March or April. He says Fed minutes show almost all officials wanting a hike, and prediction markets imply about a 23% chance of recession next year. He links Nvidia's weakness despite a strong earnings beat to SEC probes, slower circular financing and retail money moving into the Anthropic IPO. He draws parallels to 1996, when Greenspan resisted hikes citing productivity, and 2018, when a Fed pause preceded a rebound. He argues the AI bubble is still ahead and that a Fed pause would be bullish. Much of the video is promotional and is omitted. Several figures are unsourced.

glossary.title: Why investing isn't working anymore
glossary.llm_summary: Felix Nicholas Pin, presenting as an economist and former investment banker, argues that the old rules of wages plus buy-and-hold investing no longer work. His cited data: US new-house prices rose from about 2.5x to 4.5x annual income since the early 1970s; the S&P 500 is up about 60x since 1971 against roughly 9x for wages; gold is up about 100x over the same period. He shows S&P 500 real returns by era: about 11.8% a year over the last 10-12 years, losses in 2000-2012, about 15% a year in 1985-1999, and roughly zero for the 15 years before that. He notes the Nasdaq was flat for about 15 years after 2000, and that Japan took about 35 years after its 1989 peak to return to zero. He says five tech and AI-linked companies make up 30-40% of the S&P 500. He attributes the prior 40-year bull run to falling interest rates from 1981 to near zero, and says that has reversed: US inflation reached about 9%, and the average 30-year mortgage rate rose from about 2.5% in 2021 to about 7.5%. He forecasts a likely decade of weak average returns through mean reversion and says AI-profit expectations will not play out. He argues buy-and-hold only works with a horizon of 20 years or more. Most figures are given without sources. The video also promotes paid seminars and a downloadable workbook, and briefly mentions a Goldman Sachs 2027 gold report without discussing its content.

glossary.llm_summary: The speaker argues the post-midterm market swing reflected anger over AI data-center spending, not partisan politics. On Wednesday the Dow posted its best post-midterm day since 1982, while Vistra fell 14%, CoreWeave about 10% and Micron 7%, and Microsoft rose over 6%. On Thursday the Nasdaq 100 lost about $2.3 trillion, which he calls its largest one-day loss ever, the biggest semiconductor fund fell over 11%, and Reuters reported all 11 S&P 500 sectors lower with about $3 trillion wiped out. Candidates Gina Hinojosa (Texas), Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia) and Amy Acton (Ohio) campaigned on pausing data-center approvals, and voters opposed 40 of 41 data-center ballot measures across 10 states, per the speaker. Financing is central: Alphabet fell about 13% on October 29 after third-quarter capex of $51 billion exceeded roughly $42 billion of operating cash. Citing Goldman Sachs, he says hyperscalers borrowed about $296 billion in bonds this year versus $108 billion last year, with $440 billion expected next year. Debt-funded builds, often 60-80% borrowed, keep accruing interest during delays. Microsoft exited a UK AI supercomputer after power delays, and ING is reportedly selling about $500 million of data-center loans. Goldman estimates pauses could affect about 45% of planned US data-center capacity. He also cites Treasury figures that AI investment drove nearly 30% of US growth in the first three quarters, JPMorgan's estimate that AI-linked firms are close to half the S&P 500, and Fed data showing stocks at 48% of household financial assets, the highest since 1945. An Economist/YouGov poll found 82% of Democrats, 74% of independents and 59% of Republicans think AI is advancing too quickly. He ends without a firm view, seeing valid arguments on both sides.

Whoever slows down on their own becomes the one who lost the AI race, so nobody slows down, which means the only thing that can slow them down is something that slows all of them down at the same time. And on Tuesday, voters elected people who not only can do exactly that, but who are also on the record saying they want to. That's what Wall Street was cheering for on Wednesday. If the states won't let you build as fast, you can't spend as fast. For the first time since the start of the AI bubble, it looked like Big Tech might actually get put on a budget, and Wall Street loved it. It's like getting your card declined at the bar at 1:00 a.m. It's embarrassing, but it 's also the best financial decision that happened all night. Not that I'm speaking from experience or anything, because it turns out Wall Street didn't want to pay for the build out either, but there's a catch that comes with putting Big Tech on a budget. A dollar Big Tech doesn't spend is a dollar somebody else doesn't get, and that somebody else is the other half of the industry, the companies that cash the checks. The biggest semiconductor fund on the market fell more than 11% on Thursday, its worst day in six years. Nvidia alone lost about $447 billion in value, and that was three days before the news about Jensen Huang broke, which is a whole different video for a different day. Wednesday and Thursday weren't two different reactions. Nothing about the vote had changed. It was the same news read from two different sides of the same dollar. On Wednesday, the market added up how much money Big Tech might get to keep. On Thursday, it hit who that money was supposed to go to. But if this was only about chip stocks having a bad day in the market, I wouldn't be making this video. What makes this dangerous is that the companies building these data centers mostly aren't building them with their own money. It's normal for a big data center to be built with 60 to 80% borrowed money, And the plan for paying it back is simple. You finish the building, your tenant moves in, and the rent covers the debt. But the problems start to show up when the state you planned on building in starts to hit pause on things because the debt doesn't care about a pause. If your project gets frozen for a year, the interest is still due every month whether the building is finished or not. A few months ago, I made a video about how the biggest threat to the AI bubble isn't the technology failing. It's AI showing up late. Well, this is what late looks like. An unfinished data center costs more every month it sits there and it earns nothing while it does. Nvidia now puts out a new generation of AI chips about once a year. Each new generation does more work for the same money, so buyers pay less for the generation before it. A data center isn't like a house where you can leave it half built until things calm down. It's like a carton of milk. It starts to spoil the day the chips show up whether the power's on or not. And the tech giants know that, so their leases are usually built around a delivery date. If the building isn't ready in time, the tenant can walk away. The industry calls it an outside date, which sounds like a picnic in the park, but it's actually the date your tenant is legally allowed to ghost you. So if a delay pushes you past that date and your tenant decides to leave, you're left holding the debt and a room full of aging chips. And we're already seeing it happen. Last month, Microsoft walked away from Britain's largest AI supercomputer. It was supposed to switch on about 23,000 Nvidia chips early next year. Microsoft pulled out after the power connection got pushed into the 2030s. And that wasn't a moratorium. That was one late power connection. Now picture a scenario where the delay gets written into state law in the state where a quarter of these things are supposed to go. That's the difference between AI and most industries. When a business built on its own money slows down, it makes less money. When a business built on debt slows down, the question becomes who doesn't get paid back? In my last video, I showed you how the people financing the AI bubble have started buying insurance against it, the kind that pays out if a company stops paying its debts. Well, last week we saw someone take it a step further. The Dutch bank, ING, is now looking to dump about $500 million of data center loans in one of the first sales of its kind. It reflects concerns that the Democratic Party, after sweeping the US midterm elections, might impede data center developments. And banks don't usually auction off the loans they're excited about. It's the same reason nobody lists their good couch on Facebook Marketplace. They list the one they want out of the house. So the tenants have a way out written into the lease. The banks have started looking for theirs. And the debt that let the AI industry build this fast is the same debt that's making slowing down dangerous. And I know what a lot of you are thinking right now. Good. Let the chip makers and the banks burn. But the problem is the damage doesn't stop with them. And you could see that on Thursday, too. It wasn't just the chip stocks that fell that day. Reuters reported that all 11 S&P 500 sectors finished lower with an estimated $3 trillion in market value wiped out in the sell off. Remember how Wednesday was the Dow's best day after a midterm since 1982? Well, the very next day was the Dow's worst second day after a midterm since the index was created in 1896. So how does a pause on data centers hit the companies that have never been anywhere near one? It's because there's one more thing that's been living off the AI spending. It's the entire country. The day before the election, the Treasury Department put out its regular report on the economy. And by the Treasury's own measure, AI related investment accounted for nearly 30% of all the growth in the American economy over the first three quarters of this year. And that's just the economy. There's also the stock market. JP Morgan found that companies tied to AI now make up close to half of the entire S&P 500. The only time one theme has ever made up a bigger piece of the American stock market was the railroads in the 1880s. And underneath the stock market is the part that matters most, the people who own it. Stocks now make up 48% of all the financial assets American households own. That's the highest share the Federal Reserve has on record in data going back to 1945. The economy's growth is leaning on AI. The stock market is leaning on AI, and American households are leaning on the stock market more than they ever have, which means a dollar big tech doesn't spend doesn't just hurt the AI industry. Eventually, it comes out of the stocks in your retirement account. A professor at Columbia, whose name I'm not even going to try to pronounce, studies how all of this gets financed. And his conclusion was, quote, we'd basically be in a recession right now without data centers. That's how big AI is. So what happens when the thing holding up everything is the same thing everybody's trying to slow down? Well, it probably doesn't end good. That 's for sure. Goldman Sachs estimates that the pauses now passed or pledged around the country could affect about 45% of all the data center capacity planned in the United States. That's nearly half of everything on the road map. And this isn't a red team versus blue team thing either. Last month, the Economist and YouGov asked registered voters whether AI was advancing too quickly or too slowly. 82% of Democrats said it was moving too quickly. So did 74% of independents and 59% of Republicans. So if you ask America what it wants, the answer is pretty clear. The vast majority want AI to slow down. But on the other hand, AI has become the thing holding up the economy, the stock market, and according to the professor whose name I still can't pronounce, the only thing standing between us and a recession. And I want to hear what everybody else thinks about this. Leave a comment and tell me what you think we should do because I've gone back and forth on this. And honestly, I don't have a good answer. I see valid arguments on both sides. It feels like we've reached a crossroads where both sides can't win and something's going to have to give one way or another. The reality is America's economy now survives on the one thing everybody hates most. [music]

glossary.title: Lithium Torched, Gold Abandoned, Uranium Ignored (Sam Berridge)
glossary.llm_summary: Fund manager Sam Berridge (on the 'Money of Mine' podcast, 21 Nov 2026) said his portfolio is down heavily across commodities, with cash above 20% of NAV. He framed the current weakness as a financial-flow and liquidity event rather than a demand collapse. Energy: Strait of Hormuz flows are continuing, refined product shipments are rising, and the US had a diesel inventory build of about 13 million barrels in one week, its largest in roughly 20 years per the speaker. He said his fund cut oil positions in mid-June after a memorandum of understanding was announced, then re-entered, and said it should have added more. Rates: he said Australian unemployment data drove markets to price RBA cuts around mid-year. For the US, markets were pricing a near-certain Fed hike at the 8 December meeting plus two more; he is sceptical and expects at least one to be priced out within three to four months. Gold: he attributed the slide to around US$3,600 to forced liquidation for cash, and said gold tends to do well when central banks lose control of long-end yields. Copper: the Chinese physical premium is about US$420/t, which he called the highest ever, and US copper inventory is over 12 months of supply. He expects the stock to stay in the US and says the price fall reflects financial positioning. He estimated data-centre-related copper demand at about 4% of the total, so a 20-30% build-out cut would cut demand roughly 1%. He cited 2027 AI capex estimates of about US$1.4-1.5 trillion from Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley. Uranium: spot is ticking up; he cited Cameco commentary of floor pricing above US$100/lb and ceilings near US$170. He noted 68 reactors under construction globally. Rare earths: prices are described as firm; he discussed a Brazilian project and a weak raise from Pelican priced at about $7.80 and now around $6. Tungsten: he is watching China's export-restriction review, dated 10 January, and expects prices to bounce. Lithium: prices are near the bottom of the cost curve, with a possible demand pick-up in the June quarter next year. Iron ore: short interest is near a record; he is not positioned long. Currency: he said the fall in the Australian dollar has been material and that many commodities are up month-to-date in AUD terms. M&A: Guerrilla Gold's deal for IGO's Cosmos project was a tight club deal that rose 36%; he expects limited M&A while boards resist selling at the bottom. Policy: he opposed the proposed removal of the 50% capital gains discount, which he said would raise the cost of equity. He also said AGM votes against excessive director share issuance are needed. Caveats: this is an auto-generated transcript with some misspellings, and several numbers are the speaker's own, unverified figures.

glossary.title: How to Hedge THE CRASH Before It's Too Late.
glossary.llm_summary:
Speaker 'Kevin' (Meet Kevin channel) describes how he would hedge a sell-off, while stating it is not personalised advice. He says the Nasdaq 100 is negative for 2026 and has lost the 627 level, citing Sarah Eisen. He says Anthropic is down about 10% from its IPO, which he had warned about.

Gold: he is bearish. He argues Kevin Warsh's Fed nomination is bad for gold because a Warsh-led Fed would shrink its balance sheet, tightening liquidity, leading to disinflation and eventually deflation, and possibly an aggressive hiking cycle aimed at AI euphoria. He says gold was $5,000 when he turned bearish and is now about $3,500. He sees $4,000 as a ceiling and expects a '2' handle before a '5' handle. He says historically gold rallies 3 to 5 years after money printing, but shows no data.

Options: he says the VIX is at its highest level since March 27 this year. High volatility makes puts expensive, so a investor can lose money on puts even if stocks fall, if volatility compresses. In high-volatility periods he prefers selling calls.

Rates and bonds: he says he called a top in the 10-year Treasury yield at 5.27%, and that the 6-month Treasury is around 4.4%. He favours short-dated Treasuries (6 months to 2 years) for risk-free yield. He expects yields to plunge once the AI bubble pops and a labour-market recession arrives, but does not expect a cliff-like fall soon.

Real estate: he is heavily overweight, roughly 95% of his firm's allocation, and says Orlando and Tampa home prices are still falling from oversupply. He calls his position a 'triple hedge' against falling rates, an AI bust and restricted building in Democratic-led California.

Other: he says Bitcoin is a risk asset with beta near one, not a hedge. He calls China fears overblown. He cites an Iranian Revolutionary Guards statement that a tanker caught fire after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz, plus reports of explosions at Kharg Island. He cites Goldman Sachs on hedge funds degrossing. He names Apple's reported computer-use AI agent (not expected before end-2027) and healthcare names as possible hedges, some now pricey. He says he is buying dips with low equity exposure and warns against margin.

Much of the video is promotion: a paid $1,000 venture-capital fund segment, memberships, a newsletter, life insurance and a podcast. These are excluded from the claims. Most macro claims are unsourced opinion. Sourced items are the Nasdaq level, the VIX, the IRGC statement and the Goldman report.

glossary.llm_summary: Host Meet Kevin, a YouTube financial commentator, reports Nvidia down roughly 5-6% on the day, with market value near $3.3 trillion versus a prior peak above $5 trillion, and says the Nasdaq 100 is falling with it. He attributes part of the selloff to a rumor that CEO Jensen Huang could raise about $50 billion to found a new chip company. The rumor traces to a Semafor reporter's speculation after a podcast remark, and the host says it is unverified. Prediction-market odds of Huang returning as Nvidia CEO have reportedly fallen. He cites analyst Mingchi Kuo's note that Google cut 2027 Broadcom TPU 8i shipments by about one million units, a shift from inference toward training compute. He reports US approvals of roughly 3.4 million AI chips for Chinese firms led by Alibaba since May 2026, including 445,000 H200s for Tencent and 880,000 approved in total. He cites Treasury Secretary Bessent on CNBC that the largest crude volume yet has left the Strait of Hormuz, with oil down about 1.5%. The 10-year Treasury yield fell 10.6 basis points. He argues the selloff raises the odds the Federal Reserve reconsiders a December 9 hike, and he flags risks over the next two to three weeks: Iran, inflation, budget fights and an Israeli coalition dispute. He predicts an investigation into Huang will conclude between February and April, based on an average three-to-five-month timeline for CEO scandals, and forecasts a board rehire with Nvidia shares rising sharply. Much of the commentary is promotional, and the rumor claims are speculative.

glossary.llm_summary:
The video is a daily US market commentary from the 'Meet Kevin' channel, recorded during a late-November 2026 sell-off. Much of the runtime is promotion: the channel is sponsored by a prediction-market platform, a venture fund and a life insurer, and the host sells a paid course, a 'terminal' product and a Black Friday discount. Those segments are excluded here.

Market data cited: the Nasdaq 100 had turned negative year to date and was losing a support level near 627. Citing CNBC's Sarah Eisen, the host says the S&P 500 was down about 7% on the week. The VIX was described as at its highest since late March. Bitcoin broke below 60,000, which the host says has cost about $900bn of market cap over 45 days, and he flags 57,580 as a support line. Anthropic, which listed near an $83 IPO price, was down about 10-13% from its post-IPO high. Nvidia was said to have fallen from over $5 trillion to about $3 trillion in market cap, down roughly 35% over a month. The host attributes part of this to a rumour, which he calls speculation, that CEO Jensen Huang might found a chip company raising about $50bn.

China and chips: Nvidia reportedly stopped shipping H200s to China despite holding US licences. The House Foreign Affairs Committee reportedly showed applications since May covering 3.4 million chips for Chinese firms led by Alibaba, with about 880,000 approved for Alibaba and Tencent. A reported Google cut of about one million 2027 Broadcom TPU 8i units was circulating, which the host reads as a shift from inference to training compute. He calls an AMD short report alleging China-linked exposure overblown.

Rates and the Fed: the host argues tighter financial conditions are the Fed's intended effect and that it should not hike in December. He cites Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent saying the governor pushing for a 50bp December hike had dissented in favour of a 50bp cut in January, and that headline inflation is noisy because of the energy shock. The 10-year yield fell about 10.6bp on the day, which he attributes to a flight to safety.

Energy and geopolitics: the transcript describes an ongoing US-Iran conflict with the Strait of Hormuz disrupted. Bessent is quoted saying crude flows through Hormuz the previous day were the largest since the conflict began, and that Iran has no oil on the water. Reports of a tanker struck near Hormuz and explosions near Kashm Island were noted. Crude and gasoline were said to have fallen sharply since the election. The host expects the next two to three weeks to be a risk point, citing US budget fights, an Israeli coalition dispute and China chip policy.

Gold: the host is bearish. He expects Kevin Warsh's Fed to drain liquidity, says gold has fallen from about $5,000 to about $3,500, and thinks a '2' prefix is more likely than a '5'.

Forecasts and opinions: Kathy Wood (ARK) says orbital data-centre compute will fall below terrestrial costs within two years; the host calls that too optimistic. Wood also says ARK has been averaging down on Anthropic, its best-performing venture holding. The host expects Huang to return to Nvidia after a board investigation and says the board's position is 'not considering' rather than a permanent no. He also suggests Bitcoin could reach about 102,000 in the next AI-hardware cycle.

Note: the host's predictions (Huang's return, gold direction, Bitcoin target, orbital compute timing) are not backed by data in the transcript. Index levels, market caps and export-licence figures are attributed to named outlets or a congressional committee.

Presenter Felix Nicholas Pin, promoting his PIN Institute and a free live session, argues that the S&P 500 has opened green and closed red for three straight days, which he reads as institutional "distribution" selling into retail optimism. He compares this to the tops of 2008 and 2020 and notes that during a roughly 78% Nasdaq-style drawdown there were 10-20% rallies. He gives no index-level data beyond the chart shown on screen.

On the dollar, he says the GENIUS Act takes effect on 18 January, after which issuing a US dollar stablecoin without a federal or state licence becomes a criminal offence. He says Goldman Sachs, Bank of America, Citi and Visa are forming a consortium to launch a dollar-pegged stablecoin next year, with reserves held in Treasury debt and weekly government reporting. He argues programmable dollars could be tracked or frozen. He cites unnamed "big banks" forecasting the dollar about 5% weaker next year, and roughly $1 trillion of Treasury buybacks that he calls stimulus.

On metals, he says gold and silver are falling. He cites central banks officially buying over 300 tonnes in the last three months, about 40% above the prior year's pace, without a source. He shows gold well below its 200-day moving average, a gap he says is the widest in a long time, and says silver is near $41. He describes the gold/silver ratio as stretched and says options bets exist on $90 silver. He attributes some gold selling to Iran, Gulf states and oil importers such as Turkey needing cash for oil. He discloses that he owns gold and silver and trades options, and says he is not a financial adviser.

glossary.title: The Fed is Engineering a Total Stock Market Wipeout.
glossary.llm_summary: Host Kevin (Meet Kevin channel) argues the Fed may be deliberately tightening financial conditions by pushing stocks down to cool inflation, which he frames as a 'Fed problem number one.' He quotes Fed Vice Chair Bar on the risk of rapid deleveraging and self-reinforcing fire sales, citing hedge fund leverage, leveraged ETFs, options and perpetuals that don't show in margin statistics. He cites roughly $800bn of off-balance-sheet AI-firm obligations expected by year-end 2026, possibly over $3tn in nominal terms, and a financial stability report saying the equity premium over bonds is near its lowest relative to history (though not at dot-com lows). He says GPU rental rates for older chips (A100, H100, H200, B200, B300) have risen over the past 12 months, contrary to depreciation fears. On Nvidia, he notes neocloud commitments fell from $36bn to $32bn and investment outflows fell from $21bn to $11bn, and says Oracle CDS has been rising again. He quotes Warsh that AI productivity has not yet shown up and that hikes may be needed if GDP runs above trend near full employment, and St Louis Fed's Musalem saying several hikes may be needed. He reports a Bank of America fund manager survey (52% expect hyperscaler capex cuts within six months, up from 30% in October) and says Morgan Stanley cut SanDisk fiscal 2029 EPS by 21%. He says the market odds of a December hike have collapsed to about 3% after no Iran deal. The video is heavily promotional (sponsored segments, a paid $1,000 promotion, a course sales pitch) and much of the rhetoric is noise; the Fed-quote and data points are the usable part.

glossary.llm_summary: Meet Kevin, a YouTuber who calls himself a financial analyst, argues that a run of outages and cyber incidents is more than coincidence. He cites a Wall Street Journal report that Visa, Mastercard and JP Morgan customer data was leaked through outside vendors, attributed to a group he calls N, possibly ransomware and possibly Russian. He lists recent disruptions: Microsoft 365 email outages tied to a defect in a July fix, an FAA emergency ground stop, Chase and United technology issues, NSA system outages, and Apple login and Apple Pay problems. He says Costco sold 21 of its 26 largest generators within six days, which he links to stockpiling. He attributes much of the disruption to AI-driven vulnerability discovery forcing rushed patches, and reports Microsoft security fixes rising from 68 in November 2025 to 1,094 in November 2026. He says Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy requested $50 billion to avoid another ground stop. He cites an alleged North Korean theft of about $6 billion from Binance, with $2.7 billion frozen, and says Treasury sanctioned the Russia-linked payment network A7 on October 1, citing Scott Bessent. He claims Iran is linked to several incidents, including freezer failures at French stores and US military commissaries. He presents most state-actor links as allegation or rumor, and notes that officials he cites deny coordinated attacks. On markets, he says gold is at $3,679, down from $5,000, and that he is bearish on it during a Federal Reserve hiking cycle. He gives subjective odds of 85% for more outages with things mostly staying okay, and 14% for a serious attack. Sponsor segments and rumors of bank resets on November 17 are not assessed.

glossary.title: Why the oceans are being partitioned
glossary.llm_summary: Commentator Shivan (Caspian Report) argues the oceans are being partitioned through a series of exceptions rather than formal treaties. In February 2026 a US company sought permission to mine the Pacific seabed from Washington rather than the International Seabed Authority (ISA). He says the Trump administration has fast-tracked deep-sea mining permits in the Clarion Clipperton zone and opened seabed near American Samoa, a precedent China, India and Russia could cite, since all three signed the ISA rules. He states China dominates processing of many critical minerals and that the ISA has issued dozens of exploration permits in nodule-rich areas. On chokepoints he cites Iran charging Hormuz transit fees, Houthi threats in Bab el-Mandeb, Trump briefly floating a US Hormuz fee, and Indonesia's withdrawn Malacca toll proposal. He warns of higher shipping costs, less reliable supply chains and more naval spending. Most figures are not sourced.
glossary.transcript_text: In February 2026, an American company sought permission to mine minerals from the bottom of the Pacific Ocean. The proposed site lies thousands of kilometers from the United States in waters beyond any country's national jurisdiction. Under the international system governing the deep seabed, activities there are supposed to be managed collectively. But the company did not seek permission from the international body. It turned to Washington instead. The Trump administration had already moved to accelerate American seabed mining, hoping to secure valuable minerals without depending on foreign suppliers. For Washington, this made strategic sense. China dominates the processing of many critical minerals, and the United States wants alternatives. Yet, there is a larger issue here. For decades, America has been one of the strongest defenders of an international maritime system that limits what individual countries can claim or control. Its naval power has helped keep shipping routes accessible, while its diplomats have repeatedly challenged the excessive claims [music] of others. But things have changed. Washington is now breaking the rules it once helped set up. And the timing is particularly consequential because rivals elsewhere are testing the rules in their own ways. The conditions under which ships can travel, resources can be extracted, and maritime claims can be enforced are increasingly contested. Russian linked vessels are suspected of damaging undersea cables. The Houthis are threatening shipping through the Babel Mandeb. Iran is charging ships for passage through Hormuz while President Donald Trump briefly floated the idea of an American fee there as well. Even Indonesia proposed a toll system in the Strait of Malaa though the proposal was later withdrawn. No one has formally announced a new partition of the seas and that is precisely what makes it easy [music] to miss. The oceans are not being divided with lines on a map, at least not yet. Instead, the old order is being dismantled one exception at a time. When you spend a lot of time following world events, there's always another crisis to understand, another conflict to follow. And between alarming headlines, endless commentary, and the temptation to keep doom scrolling, it's easy to feel overwhelmed by everything happening around us. I caught myself in that spiral recently, just scrolling through updates late at night, one headline after another. At some point, you're no longer staying informed. You're just feeding the anxiety. Talking through moments like these with a therapist, can really help set healthier boundaries. Better Help, today's paid partner, makes starting therapy easier. You just answer a few questions through a quiz and get matched with a credentialed therapist. Sessions can take place by phone, video, or text, depending on what you're most comfortable with. And if your therapist isn't the right fit, you can switch at no extra cost. With insurance options from BetterHelp, therapy may be more affordable than you think with co-pays as low as $15. For BetterHelp members in the United States, therapy may cost less with insurance options available through select health plans. Many members pay $15 or less, and some pay nothing at all. And if you don't have insurance or live outside the United States, you can still get 10% off your first month. Just follow the link in the description or visit betterhelp.com/caspian report to get started. [music] Almost every piece of land on Earth belongs to someone. Borders cut through mountains, grasslands, [music] forests, and rivers. But the oceans are different. Most remain outside national boundaries, open to ships from almost anywhere. That openness was by choice. As naval technology improved during the 20th century, the leading [music] powers gained the ability to patrol distant waters and enforce claims far from their shores. [music] A country might reasonably want to protect its offshore resources and defend its coastline, but allowing governments to restrict every passage near their shores would have made international trade exceedingly difficult. [music] The solution was a compromise between the economic rights of coastal states and the navigational freedoms of everyone else. For [music] decades, that arrangement served the United States particularly well. American merchant ships could reach markets around the world, while the US Navy could operate across distant waters without constantly seeking permission from foreign governments. Washington [music] never ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, partly because of objections to its seabed [music] mining provisions, but it nevertheless supported many of the Convention's principles. [music] Keeping the oceans open was ultimately more valuable than trying to control every choke point. However, the system had a built-in flaw. International tribunals can determine legal rights, but they cannot enforce their judgments through force. [music] The UN Security Council could impose sanctions or authorize action to protect shipping [music] except that China, Russia, and the United States can each block such decisions with a veto. That leaves enforcement largely in the hands of individual governments, including those accused of violating the rules. China [music] has spent much of the past 20 years exploiting this flaw. Beijing claims maritime rights across waters also claimed by neighboring countries including the Philippines. [music] In 2016, an international tribunal rejected China's claims beyond what the law of the sea permits. Beijing, however, refused to accept the ruling and continued strengthening its presence through artificial islands and naval deployments. [music] For the Philippines, this created a dangerous reality. International law recognized Philippine maritime rights, but exercising them was another matter. Chinese vessels could obstruct fishing [music] boats, disrupt resupply missions, and make operating in contested waters increasingly risky. Manila could appeal to international institutions and seek support from its allies, but the tribunal itself had no means of forcing Beijing to comply. And this is where the distinction between legal rights and physical control becomes [music] crucial. Beijing does not need the international community to recognize the South China Sea [music] as its territory. By maintaining a powerful military and coast guard presence, Beijing can influence who operates in disputed areas and under what conditions. Over time, that practical influence can become increasingly difficult to reverse, even if the underlying claims remain legally contested. Washington has repeatedly pushed back against this policy by conducting freedom of navigation operations. America's [music] concern is understandable. If powerful coastal states can decide which foreign vessels are allowed to operate in surrounding waters, American naval mobility would become increasingly vulnerable to political restrictions. [music] And since the US Navy underpins American power projection, restricting its movement would thereby diminish Washington's influence. On the flip side though, China's position is also understandable. It depends enormously on international shipping. Its [music] factories require raw materials from distant suppliers while its [music] exports travel through waters controlled or influenced by others. Beijing therefore benefits from the open seas even as it seeks greater control over certain regions. This then exposes a predicament at the heart of the maritime order. Governments may defend international rules for decades only to challenge them when those same rules stand in the way of something they consider strategically essential. And China [music] is hardly alone. Iran, Russia, Turkey, Britain, Canada, Norway, and Australia have all challenged aspects of the maritime order in pursuit of their own interests. [music] But the consequences are not equal. The laws of the sea are only effective when powerful states find it convenient to obey them. For everyone else, the rules are merely polite suggestions. This is where Delta Sweep comes in. On its live map, every country's exclusive economic zone is drawn alongside shipping routes, the ocean floor, and choke points. Meanwhile, Navy ships are tracked by class, from carrier strike groups to amphibious vessels, and incidents appear where they unfold. [music] And for those short on time, the recap feature condenses the past 24 hours into a [music] brief animated tour of the globe. Explore this and more at delta sweep.com. Up to this point, the pressure has been on shipping lanes and choke points, but the partition of the oceans is widening. Countries are interested [music] not only in controlling what moves on the surface, but also what lies underneath. Huge areas of the Pacific and Indian oceans contain [music] polytallic nodules rich in valuable minerals. Among the biggest deposits are the Clarion Clipperton zone between Hawaii and Mexico, the central Indian Ocean Basin, and [music] the Penin Basin in the South Pacific. The International Seabed Authority has already issued dozens of permits allowing governments and companies [music] to explore these areas, map deposits, and test extraction methods. The only thing preventing a freefor-all mining frenzy is that lawmakers cannot seem to agree on environmental safeguards. Much of the deep ocean remains poorly understood and large-scale mining could damage ecosystems that scientists have barely begun to study. But Washington is unwilling to wait. Since the United States never joined the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, it is [music] technically not bound by it. As such, the Trump administration has fast-tracked [music] permits for deep sea mining in the Clarion Clipperton zone and is opening the seabed near American Samoa for exploration and commercial extraction. Washington may see that as a way to secure resources outside China's control, but other powers see something else, a precedent. China, India, and Russia have all signed onto international rules governing seabed extraction. [music] If the United States begins mining independently of those rules, Beijing and Moscow [music] can point to Washington the next time they want an exception or seek alternative arrangements of their own. So, American [music] unilateralism gives competitors a legit justification to disregard maritime rules when it suits them. And that may [music] be the most important element of the entire partition. Ocean governance is unlikely to collapse because every country suddenly tears up the same treaty. It is [music] more likely to die through a succession of smaller exceptions. One country charges ships, another restricts passage, a third minds a disputed seabed, and some just ignore tribunal rulings. Each president makes the next one slightly easier to defend. [music] And once that becomes the norm, it will not stop with shipping lanes or minerals. Governments could become more aggressive over fishing grounds, subsea cables, [music] and strategically located islands. The waters surrounding Taiwan, Swalbard, Cyprus, and even Greenland could all become fair play. The eventual consequences could be [music] worldchanging. Ships forced to take longer routes or pay more fees would make trade [music] more expensive. Supply chains would become less reliable, while governments controlling choke points could gain greater leverage over food, energy, and strategic resources. Every disputed island or seabed could become a flash point on its own. That in turn would put a premium on naval power. Countries hoping to defend or enforce maritime claims would need larger and more capable fleets. That means more surface warships and a greater naval industrial capacity. As the partition of the oceans gathers momentum, naval power would once again become one of the clearest ways to turn a claim on paper into [music] control at sea. We've seen this story before. The conquest and division of land rewarded countries that arrived first or were strong enough to defend what they claimed. >> [music] >> Borders then shifted repeatedly as empires rose and fell. And it took centuries of war and state building for most of those boundaries to stabilize. [music] The oceans escaped much of that history because governments eventually decided they gained more from [music] keeping them open than from fighting over every piece of water. If that understanding [music] breaks down, the law of the sea may give way to a much older rule, the law of the jungle. I've been your host, Shivan from Caspian Report. He says Israel's pressure is tied to its December 6 government-formation deadline. Israeli officials claim Iran is advancing chemical and biological weapons and may fit them to drones to target US officials or troops. Trump told Fox News Iran was looking at gas and bio weapons without providing evidence, and said 'if it does happen, we will wipe them out.' Per the Wall Street Journal (as of Nov 15), Iran still has roughly 1,500-2,500 missiles despite damage to production. Israel estimates 1,500-2,000 remain, from about 3,000 at the war's start. The NYT reports Iran may be using dams and tunnels to conceal missile sites. US posture: about three carriers were in the region, one (George Washington) is departing, B-1/B-2 bombers are on four-day deployment notice, and about 53,000 troops are present. The Pentagon and State Department are reportedly withdrawing troops from some bases and reloading Israel's Patriot batteries. On Congress, Democrats are debating whether to use appropriations to block Iran operations and whether to act in December or January, while avoiding a shutdown. Schumer backs using the power of the purse but has not set timing. On oil, Gulf exports reportedly recovered to 74% of pre-war levels as of Nov 13, and the IEA suggests a possible supply surplus. Estimates of about 24 million barrels a day in October were volatile due to tanker strikes. Oil is around $92, which the speaker reads as markets not pricing war risk. The rest of the transcript is sponsor segments and domestic political commentary, which are out of scope.

glossary.llm_summary:
Commentary by Kevin Prah (Meet Kevin) on the macro and market backdrop as of mid-November 2026. On Iran, the speaker says Iran is retaliating against US pressure (Operation Iron Gate, a Caspian and Hormuz blockade) with drone and ship attacks, and the US has struck Kharg-area targets near Hormuz. He argues the odds of a near-term deal fell after the US election. On oil, he cites Bloomberg for global supply above pre-war levels, Brent down over $26 in three weeks to under $92, and diesel crack spreads falling to about $40 from a normal $10-20 range. He reads this as easing inflation expectations, alongside Fed Governor Waller reportedly floating 50bp of hikes. He expects a Warsh-led Fed to weigh on gold, and says gold has underperformed.

On positioning, per the Bank of America fund manager survey, 3% of investors expect recession. Expectations of an AI capex cut within six months rose from 15% in September to 30% in October and 52% now. Net long US semis fell from 55% (September) to 45% (October) to 39%, and hedge funds are at a roughly three-standard-deviation net short in US semis. Investors favour international equities (36%) over US (24%), with 17% picking gold. Morgan Stanley reports 65% of Russell 3000 stocks down more than 20% since June, and says its capitulation indicator is near major lows (comparable to Lehman levels). Its base-case S&P 500 target is 8,700 and bull case 10,000 within 12 months, versus the index near 7,300. It sees oil falling to $75 by Q4 2027, core inflation settling near 2.5% by end-2027, and the Nasdaq 100 at a roughly 100-year-low valuation. It favours hyperscalers and AI adopters, and expects combined hyperscaler and neocloud capex to still grow about 14% into 2028.

Goldman Sachs, per the speaker, sees money flowing into consumer discretionary and staples. The speaker argues Microsoft trades near a 1x PEG despite selling compute to ByteDance, and says the Commerce Department's interim export-licensing rule lets US-headquartered firms sell AI compute abroad. He also cites reporting that Nvidia sales staff helped Alibaba access chips via Southeast Asia, and says Jensen Huang and Nvidia's Congressional testimony is expected in early December. Prediction-market odds on Huang returning as CEO are about 10%. The speaker discloses a small personal position on that bet and holds a bullish near-term view on Broadcom around $355. Much of the transcript is promotional content for the speaker's products, which is excluded here.

glossary.llm_summary: A long, promotional daily market stream by the channel host Kevin, who sells paid courses and a subscription terminal and says he holds a small position on Nvidia's CEO returning. Most of the content is about Nvidia, but the macro-relevant parts are these. Brent crude was reported under $92 a barrel, down more than $26 over three weeks, and diesel crack spreads had fallen to about $40 a barrel. That is still above the usual $10 to $20 range but is treated as a sign that supply concerns are easing after the Strait of Hormuz disruption. The host says the US is running a naval blockade and an 'Operation Iron Gate' against Iran, and that Iran is responding by attacking tankers and strikes on IRGC sites, including on Kashm Island. He calls this a stalemate with no deal likely while Trump has little motivation to negotiate. On rates, he cites Fed funds futures pricing a quarter-point hike in December, with a further hike likely in January. Governor Waller reportedly argued for faster hikes, with annualised inflation near 3.5%. Five-year breakeven inflation is described as low. He argues the combination of Fed hikes and tighter financial conditions is a difficult backdrop for equities. Bank of America's fund manager survey is cited: 52% expect an AI capex cut within six months, up from 15% in September and 30% in October, and long positions in US semiconductors fell to 39% from 55% in September. Hedge funds are described as three standard deviations short US semis. Morgan Stanley's Mike Wilson is cited with an S&P 500 base-case target of $8,700 and a bull case of $10,000 within 12 to 14 months, against an index level near $7,300. Its capitulation indicator is said to be close to a major low, near Lehman-era levels. Morgan Stanley is also quoted as seeing the Nasdaq 100 valuation at a 100-year low. The host argues that a new Commerce interim final rule on AI chip exports, which licenses sales to Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Brazil but exempts US-headquartered end users, benefits US hyperscalers such as Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Oracle. He says ByteDance is in talks for roughly $500 million of additional Microsoft cloud spending. On Anthropic's IPO, he cites reported institutional and retail orders of about $500 billion and a possible pricing above $80 a share. He predicts the stock will trade above $100 on debut. He notes that IPO price ranges are often set low to drive demand. Other items include a cluster of IT outages at Microsoft, the FAA, Chase, Apple and the NSA. The host attributes these to patching and maintenance, and cites an FBI warning that hackers are using AI tools to speed up attacks. Several figures and quotes are sourced to Bloomberg, Wall Street Journal, New York Times and Goldman and Morgan Stanley notes, but the host often paraphrases loosely and some figures, such as the oil price drop and the rate-probability percentages, are internally inconsistent in the transcript. Nothing about the Australian dollar, iron ore, copper, gold prices or the ASX is substantive. The most relevant macro content is oil and diesel supply easing, the Fed hiking path, the AI-capex and semiconductor risk-off positioning, and Iran escalation.
